rows.subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
rows.description: A student used to flexible timings arrives thirty minutes late to a meeting in a strict-time culture and is thought unreliable. Understanding the local clock, and telling people ahead, prevents offence.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 7–12, 13–17, 23–26

rows.subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
rows.description: A young professional hearing blunt criticism from a foreign manager feels hurt, though the manager means only clarity. Asking about intent and separating tone from content helps learning.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
rows.description: A traveller or worker asks locals about greetings, gifts, dress and taboos before assuming meaning. Curiosity and humility prevent errors and win warmth in any country.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
rows.description: A young Indian abroad notices that head-wobbling, personal questions about salary or marriage, and loud phone calls may surprise hosts. Explaining kindly and adapting a little helps both sides enjoy the exchange.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
rows.description: A child repeats that a group is greedy or lazy, echoing what was heard at home. The child has no evidence, only borrowed words; a calm question such as how do you know helps.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
rows.description: A child laughs at jokes about a region, faith or accent because friends do. Laughing feels like belonging, though the joke may hurt someone present; a friend who does not laugh shows another way.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: amusement, nostalgia, resentment, hurt

rows.subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
rows.description: A teenager is told all people from their state or community are a certain way, and feels unseen. Being treated as an individual matters greatly; gently correcting and finding supportive peers help.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
rows.description: A teenager notices that films show certain groups as villains, servants or comic relief, and starts to spot patterns. Asking who is missing from the story is a first step toward critical viewing.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
rows.description: A young adult realises they assumed a stranger would behave a certain way based on dress or name, and felt uneasy. Noticing a bias honestly, without self-punishment, is how it begins to weaken.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 23–26

rows.subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
rows.description: A young adult praised as naturally good at maths or as hardworking because of community feels pressure and an inability to fail. Even praise can box people in; correcting it kindly keeps the person free.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 23–26
